[b]Pronoun Palace[/b] is great satire - it's provocative without pandering, and knows how to hammer a point home while also not taking itself too seriously. It's got addictive music, excellent writing, and a wholly original style. More than any of those things, though, it's just a really freakin' good word puzzle game in a genre that doesn't get nearly as much love as it should. I showed it to my dog and it cured his transphobia. You are now at the end of my review.

If you don’t care about my viewpoints on this game’s politics and why they’ve prompted me to give this game a negative review, read this current textblock and read no further. The general meat of this game is pretty good. It’s fun, it works, You're unlikely to run into any bugs. The music is REALLY good and is one of my high praises. It’s in my opinion a bit overpriced for its current level of content and the itemization is in need of some TLC (For how relatively small the item pool is everything either slots into the realm of “run saving” or “borderline worthless.”) and the overall balancing could use a touch-up so you actually feel powerful by the end of a run. But as a bookworm roguelike, it’s fine. It’s whatever. It won’t blow your jorts off but it's a nice slower-paced brain teaser if the sensory overload simulators the genre is infested with these days are too much for you. —----------------- (disclaimer: this review section regarding content in the game was compiled from both personal experience with the game and accounts from internet mutuals who had also played it. However, all actual opinions are my own) Now, if your reading below the above line, I assume your here for the scary:™: stuff. (Full disclosure: I am approaching this game’s overt politics from a transfeminist perspective. It’s clearly an angry game that wishes to say something. And as such I intend to listen too it, and respond in accord.) Ah, pronoun palace, woke bookworm. When I first saw your trailer a month ago I was kind of pumped. It looked fun, the music was a jam. And I bought it very shortly after it released. Some of the stuff I encountered started to make my tilt my eyebrow a bit, but it wasn’t until I sat down and had a yap about it with some fellow transfeminists that some glaring issues in this game’s narrative really started to show themselves. The problem with not liking games like this politically is that from an outward perspective it looks like I’m making my bed with and easy to dismiss my opinion as being in cahoots with self-described ‘anti-woke’ morons like the starfield pronouns guy. I would like to make it apparent if my above disclaimer did not make it clear: I am a wokescold leftist and a transfem. And that is the lense through which I am treating this game. Alright, let’s cut to the chase: this game’s transfeminist narrative side is written like a tme’s idea of what transfeminist progressivism is. The main overt intended theme of the game - as indicated by every character being transgender and forcibly detransitioned by the dystopian state - is that transitioning is an uphill battle regardless of what way your going. Perhaps unintentionally, this message is contrasted by the fact that one of the transmasc characters (the child) is by far the easiest of the bunch to win a run with on account of their starting item hole punch being quite overpowered. As well as the narrative insinuations of the transmasc being able to transition in childhood while the transfem characters are all stuck transitioning in their 30’s. Could you not imagine a transfem at any other age? Does one of them wear programming socks as well? Next off there’s the ‘retransitioning’ mechanic. Put simply, spell ‘transitioning’ during a run and the character’s model will permanently change based on what way they’re transitioning. On paper, it sounds cute and serves the game’s narrative well. In practice, it’s half-assed. Most of the time it manifests in a character’s hair getting longer or them losing their beard (which I have to admit even in the context of them being a transfem forcibly detransitioned by the government, is kind of a weird trait to give them in the first place.). Assuming there aren’t any further stages, by the end the only character who looks like they’ve meaningfully changed is the transmasc character. Everyone else (read: the transfems) look… maybe like they’d be a few months into transition? Maybe? There’s other stuff too. For the ‘paddlers’ enemy, the ‘yaoi’ toothpaste guy has breasts while the ‘yuri’ woman has a flat chest, the ‘anti-sex worker’ enemy’s codex entry has a weird thing about them being kept on hormones ‘to remain fertile and youthfully bleeding’ In a way that comes off as very “Wouldn’t it be ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up if people hated trans women so much they looped around to hating ACTUAL women?”. Oh yeah, and one of the POC characters in the game is an enemy who has a variant (called ‘parasite’ in game) who’s codex entry insinuates she steals the blood of ‘svelte elf-like twinks’. To be perfectly frank, my overall view of PP is that it’s a game that’s fun to play with a bopper soundtrack but one who’s messaging I refuse to take seriously. I don’t say any of this with any particular venom towards the transfem developer, nor am I going to pretend I know her in any capacity whatsoever, but I’m more than intimately familiar with the notion that the alternate to being hugboxed by liberal steam reviewers who don’t see the problematic elements past their ability to type slurs and the wacky-zany character designs is harassment (Possibly by said liberal steam reviewers if she becomes socially acceptable to harass), or 4tran. If I were to make an earnest plea to a game I think has genuine potential, it’d be that they sit down and do some due-diligence learning, adding more POC can be done, changing the codex entires to be less transmisogynistic/racist can be done, unlearning the social biases that put the notion those were acceptably woke things to put in your woke game takes time. I understand this review is harsh, but please see it as an earnest request to righten things up, because you don’t know when the people patting your back for a job well done today will be saying you always gave them 4chan/fashy vibes on bluesky tomorrow.

This game has a lot to offer, and it is--in my humble opinion--a definitive MUST PLAY for anyone even remotely into word games. Would give it a neutral vote if I could, but giving a negative because I feel that the current overwhelmingly positive review score is a bit too strong (and, quite frankly, is probably inflated based on the surface theme of the game alone). I'd give this game a 6/10. The basic gameplay concept is strong, but gets repetitive fast and there isn't a lot of variety in playstyle / enemies / items / character selection / general uniqueness of each run, especially compared to Balatro, which seems like the default comparison for this game. A lot of the tile gimmicks are just "you need to use this tile to avoid damage" or "this tile gives more points than normal" with very minor variations, most of the items are either very strong or pretty much useless with not much in between, and likewise each character is a fairly minor change from the last that doesn't majorly impact how each run feels. Beyond gameplay, the music is excellent and the artstyle and animations are charming enough. The writing is earnest but very blunt and uninspired. The setting is lifted pretty much entirely whole cloth from 1984 and a lot of the political commentary (as a case in point, one enemy is a fat pig in a suit that hits you over the head with anvils labeled "POLITICS", "EPHEBOPHILIA", "ECONOMY", etc.) is incredibly unsubtle and mostly feel like they were written by a 10th grader who finds toilet humor hilarious and who just read 1984 and found it lifechanging. That said, though, I empathize with a lot of the angst and frustration at the current experience of living as a genderqueer person that's all over this game. All in all I don't regret the purchase and I think it's a solid game with good bones that I would happily endorse at a lower price point, but I just found myself not agreeing with some of the effusive praise this game has received for its price tag and wanted to throw my two cents in.

I should start by addressing the green invertebrate in the room. I adored Bookworm Adventures growing up - easily one of my favourites in the PopCap catalogue. Its mechanics, story, and characters make it a great experience from start to finish. Admittedly, some encounters could feel a bit redundant at times, but overall it's an experience I'd recommend if it were still commercially available. Pronoun Palace, to me, is what happens when someone uses the bones of Bookworm Adventures' gameplay to kick your teeth in. For one, this game's narrative is Woke with a capital W. It's not a simple cosmetic flair or a passing mention - this game puts its entire chest into its message. Pronoun Palace isn't afraid to make its commentary on-the-nose, much as it isn't afraid to flaunt its more provocative sense of humour. And in this day and age, honestly? Thank God. As a roguelike, the game also benefits hugely from the depth and diversity (hah) of its mechanics. It has broad selections of playable characters, spells, tile effects, enemy encounters, you name it - all with more to come in future updates. You may find a favourite playstyle, but the game has enough variety baked in that it'd be nigh impossible to find yourself going through the exact same motions, run after run. It's apparently been said that the developers wanted to staunchly oppose the standard roguelike fare of gameplay boiling down to "number go up" - and for this gameplay loop, it was 100% the correct choice. To boot, the aesthetic of Pronoun Palace has been crafted wonderfully. The artstyle is simple to grasp and incredibly expressive in the same stroke. The soundtrack in particular is a massive highlight, in my eyes. RENREN does a fantastic job at capturing a multitude of energies. These songs can contemplative, playful, bombastic, foreboding - the one constant is that they'll always be a delight. In short, Pronoun Palace benefits from every bold decision it makes. It's entirely unashamed to be what it is - that being, fun to play, fun to replay, and about as far to the left as your Tab key is. If the latter really is a dealbreaker for you, I'm sorry that you're missing out on what might be the best spiritual successor Bookworm Adventures could ever have hoped for.

Everything about this game is refreshing. From a gameplay standpoint, it’s the most intentionally-designed roguelike I’ve played in a long while. In a world saturated with “Balatro-but”s that clumsily hawk common idioms of the genre, this game is utterly surgical about what is and isn’t here. It makes for a game where every mechanic, enemies and spells alike, is a fun and interesting new puzzle to solve. There’s not a single thing here that feels unfair, bloated, or sloggy. And then from a queer art standpoint, GOD is it nice to play something that doesn’t automatically assume I’m an emotionally-exhausted escapist looking for a cozy coffee shop free from the concept of hate crimes. It’s queer media that nips and scratches when you try to pet it, but approaches real world queer issues with youthful vigor and levity rather than the anger of a tired activist. And beyond those two massive things it gets right, it’s also great for its really flexible time commitment. You can spend hours on multiple runs in a row, or just do half a fight while you drink your morning tea. Overall, phenomenal and highly recommended. This is a must-play and an instant classic.

on one end, i do like the game's satire, that's all i can really say even as a transfem. i do think its effective edgy satire that, while it is in-you-face, is also not overbearing or intrusive. nor does it ever feel overly 4tran edgy, which i'm thankful for. it mostly keeps to its framing as a dystopian satire. on the OTHER end, though... i love this game's approach to game design. i went on a journey to find the perfect roguelike for me, and i walked through so many brainless Balatro-likes. i hate the progression of all these Balatro-like-roguelikes that have appeared recently. Pronoun Palace gets two things right: 1) it actually challenges my ability to think instead of my ability to "find optimal items to assemble a meta strategy that will automatically win for me like 99% of all other roguelikes" which actually makes it feel engaging to find words. i love a game with no progression, it means all your growth comes from you, and i appreciate the rejection of standard roguelike relics and card design stuff. and 2) it makes me actually wanna engage with the game mechanics instead of always trying to avoid or optimize everything away. this game has EXCELLENT enemy design from the perspective of making you actually engage with an enemy's gimmick. i'll take this over the 100's of games that make enemies that instantly ♥♥♥♥ you over and make you never wanna engage with anything again outside of the most safe, boring cheese strategy. this game was the endpoint of my roguelike/roguelite journey, this was it, the game i've been searching for this entire time. AND it's gay on top of that, what a win/win.
